title: Trifid Nebula (Wide Field Camera 3 Image)
caption: A close-up of the Trifid Nebula (M20), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Trifid Nebula, Messier 20 · constellation Sagittarius · about 5,000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Rust-colored clouds of gas and dust, dark brown in places like mud, fill this Hubble view of the Trifid Nebula, a stellar nursery some 5,000 light-years away. The top left glows bright blue where the least dust remains, and the far-right corner is nearly pitch black where dust is densest. Bright orange stars are scattered across the scene.

Massive stars outside the frame have shaped the region for at least 300,000 years. Their ultraviolet light makes nearby gas glow, and their winds blow a huge bubble that clears and compresses the dust. Near the top of a head-shaped cloud with two horns, yellow gas flows upward as the cloud is torn apart. The left horn belongs to Herbig-Haro 399, a jet of plasma that a young protostar buried in the head has fired out periodically over centuries.

Hubble first observed this scene in 1997. Comparing the two views lets researchers measure how fast the outflows move and how much energy the protostar injects. Over millions of years the gas and dust will disappear, leaving only stars.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in visible light, with the narrow-band filters F502N shown in blue, F656N in green and F673N in red.
understand.eye: This is visible light, but each filter isolates a narrow band, and the densest dust still hides the protostars forming inside it.

explore: The darker, more triangular horn on the right hosts another young star at its tip, marked by a faint red dot with a tiny jet. A green arc above it may be a disc around the star being eroded by ultraviolet light. Near the center, a rippling line running from orange to red appears to move between the two epochs and may be a jet from another star buried in dust. The image marked Hubble's 36th launch anniversary.
